I am 70 years old and have worked these 2 mu in Quzhou for half a century. My schooling ended at primary, but the land has taught me everything worth knowing. It is just me and my wife in the household now, so I keep my plans practical and within what my back and her cooking schedule can handle. I have a well, which means I can irrigate when the heavens withhold rain, but pumping costs electricity and effort, so I do not waste a single drop.

The winter wheat I sowed last autumn is already in the ground. I planted an improved variety that has never let me down on this soil. Now that spring has arrived, I will topdress it with urea when it greens up to push the tillers, then irrigate three times from my well: at jointing, at heading, and once more during grain filling if the sky stays dry. I will spray herbicide once in early spring before the weeds take over, and fungicide once at heading to keep disease off the ears. I expect about 450 kg per mu, which is honest grain for this small plot.

After the wheat harvest in early June, I will not rest long. I will rotary till the stubble while the ground is still loose and plant hybrid maize seed from the county supply station. The summer window is short, so speed matters. I will put down compound fertilizer at planting and then topdress with urea when the maize reaches knee height. I will irrigate twice: once when it shoots up, and again when the ears are filling. Two sprays will do—herbicide after planting, and insecticide only if I see corn borers in the stalks. I expect around 500 kg per mu.

I do not believe in emptying my pockets for extra fertilizer to chase a record yield. At my age, steady harvests, healthy soil, and enough grain for my household matter more than gambling on bags of chemicals. My well water and fifty years of watching the clouds are enough if I time the work right.
